p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for nearly nine months, and the countdown clock says 506.
Over the summer the program became one team across two planets, seventeen people including five engineers on Ares Station led by Chiamaka Okonkwo.
Sam kept Ada's logs private, as she asked, and asked the readiness board for an independent check of the station's oxygen margin.
In a hardware store in Strasburg, Bea Kowal told Sam that AR 2207 was closed in a twenty two minute meeting in 2059, and she later sent the board a written statement.
AR 2207 is still open, and on September 29 the first autonomy build flew the departure burn in simulation with nobody's hands on anything, once in nine runs.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, with four kids in Aurora.
Ruth Calder. On the readiness board, and the Petrel's flight director.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Ada Okafor. Sam's daughter on Ares Station.
Frances Odum. Chair of Families of Ares.
Chiamaka Okonkwo. Breather operations lead on Ares Station.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Peg Sato. Tallgrass contracts and procurement.
Nell Garrity. Aldergrove's account lead, the "valve lady." She brought her company's Petrel records, carried for twenty six years.
New in this chapter: Thandi Mokoena and Dr. Anjali Rao.

Friday, September 30, 2061. 6:40 AM. The simulator bay still smelled of last night: cold coffee, warm electronics, and the marker Rafa had used to write ONCE on the inside of the door, in letters a foot high. Sam had come in early to read the run logs before anybody could tell him what they meant. Somebody had beaten him to it.

Commander Yusra Haddad was in the left seat of the mockup with the lights down and the departure burn on the screen in front of her, flying it by hand. Ignition, nineteen minutes against the simulated Earth, cutoff. She reset it and flew it again. He stood at the back by the door, where she'd stood the night before, and counted. She flew it nine times. Nine for nine. On the last one she trimmed the burn a little late and then exactly right, the way the guidance had on run one, and he understood that she'd been watching the software last night as closely as it had been watching the ship.

She pulled the headset off and saw him. Rafa says once is a fact and twice is a capability, she said. I'm a capability. I've got a plane to Houston at ten. She picked up her bag. At the door she stopped and looked at the word on it for a while, and didn't say anything about it, and went.

Rafa's sixty engineers worked in two week sprints with a demo every other Friday. The autonomy squad was nine of them, at the software end of the cafeteria and the far end of the sim bay, and they'd built A1 in five sprints since July. Under ONCE, smaller, somebody had written the squad's velocity for each of those sprints in story points: 34, 28, 31, 37, 26. Nobody outside the squad had ever asked to see the column.
At 7:15 Rafa sent a page to Sam, Quinn, and Hana.

HALCYON FLIGHT SOFTWARE AUTONOMY A QUESTION FOR RELEASE A2 R. QUINTERO SEPTEMBER 30 2061. BUILD A1 FLEW THE DEPARTURE BURN IN SIM ONCE IN NINE RUNS. IT WAS BUILT TO HELP A CREW. IT TURNS OUT IT CAN NEARLY FLY ONE PART OF THE TRIP WITHOUT ONE.. QUESTION FOR THE PROGRAM: IF THE CREW CAN'T FLY IN THE WINDOW (AN INJURY, AN ILLNESS, A CREW LAUNCH THAT SLIPS PAST MARCH 4), CAN HALCYON GO ANYWAY, UNCREWED, AND DELIVER THE BREATHER?. TODAY THE ANSWER IS NO. THE BACKLOG HAS 1,140 ITEMS IN IT AND NONE OF THEM ASKS THAT QUESTION.. I'D LIKE TO ASK IT. I NEED SOMEBODY TO TELL ME WHAT GOES FIRST.

Garrett answered at 7:42, to everyone. Love the energy. The crew is the product. Let's not build a ship that makes the crew optional. At 8:05 Hale's chief of staff, who had been copied by somebody, wrote to Sam alone. The Director would like to understand whether Halcyon can "fly itself," and how soon she can say so.

Sam read both of them twice. Then he read the last line of Rafa's again. I need somebody to tell me what goes first. In nineteen years of running a building he had never once had to decide what mattered most in somebody else's software. He'd only had to keep the lights on while they decided.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 506.

Monday, October 3. The flight software backlog lived in a tool on Rafa's laptop and, more and more, in Rafa's head. Eleven hundred and forty items. Quinn had pulled the request history for September and printed it out on the big room table, and the printout hung off both ends.

Requests came from everywhere. The Director's office had added nine items in September, all marked high. Garrett had added four through his assistant, all marked urgent, one of them a boot screen with the mission patch on it. Hana had added two about the valve model. Okonkwo's station engineers had added six about the Breather's alarms, through the morning packet. Commander Haddad had added thirty one, all from demos, every one a thing that would have killed her. Rafa had ordered all of it himself, at night, and reordered it whenever somebody senior walked past his desk.
I build it, Rafa said. I shouldn't also be the one who decides what it's for. I've been doing both and I'm doing the second one badly.
Garrett, on the speaker from his car: Then you decide, Sam. Program manager. One throat to choke.

Sam didn't think it should be his throat. He thought it should be the person who'd have to sit on the ship. At noon he called Haddad in Houston, on the first full day of a week of training, and asked her. She said yes before he'd finished asking. Then she asked what she'd be the owner of, exactly. Who can change my order? And who gets to call you when they don't like it?
Her calendar for October had eleven free hours in it.

He writes it on one page that afternoon and sends it to every lead and to the Director's office. Who orders the backlog: Haddad, and only Haddad. Who can ask: anyone, by convincing her. Who sizes: the developers. What Sam does: clears her calendar and backs her when somebody senior calls. Then he spends Tuesday with the crew office in Houston and gets her two days a week at Watkins through March, which also means two nights a week at home in Aurora. She sends one line about that. My husband says thank you. So do I. Rafa prints the Scrum Guide's sentence about convincing the product owner and tapes it to his monitor. I'm going to enjoy reading that to Garrett.

Tuesday, October 4. Haddad had been product owner for one day, and her first act was a question she sent to Sam, Rafa, Quinn, and Hana at 6:02 AM from a hotel in Houston. Before I order anything: what is the autonomy release for? I need one sentence.
Nobody had one. They had four.

Rafa's was everything: every phase of the flight, every fault the ship could have, a crew optional ship by the end of 2062. Garrett's was the sentence he'd already said to his investors on Friday afternoon, Halcyon can fly itself, the same three words Hale's chief of staff had used that morning. Hana's was quieter. She'd rather the squad spent the year on the crew's displays and the valve model, the things the crew would actually use, and let the uncrewed idea sit in a drawer. Nobody's going to fly my stage without a crew on it, she said. That's a slide.

Quinn's wasn't a sentence. It was arithmetic. The crew launched up to the ship in January 2063. If they couldn't go, for any reason, an injury, an illness, a crew launch that slipped, the window closed on March 4 with the Breather still circling the Earth. On the worst number anybody had, the colony couldn't wait twenty six months for the next one. On the agency's own number it couldn't either.
Quinn had written it on a sticky note and stuck it to Sam's monitor. WHAT IF THE CREW CAN'T GO?
The program's change board met on Wednesdays.

They write the sentence together on the big room whiteboard, Haddad on the screen from Houston. Release A2 makes it possible for Halcyon to fly the Breather to Mars and land it without a crew, if it has to, by the time the crew would have to commit to fly. Under it, what the smallest version must do: depart, coast, correct, capture at Mars, hand off the lander, land it. Crude in every phase, whole from one end to the other. Quinn and the squad size it at 286 points. It fits inside the software release plan if the crew display work moves later, so the change is to the release plan and the integrated plan and not to the budget, and on Wednesday it goes to the change board with what moves, what it costs the crew, and what the program gets for it: a second way through the window. The board approves it with one condition, Hana's. It's written down everywhere as an option, and never as the plan. Haddad reads the minutes and sends one line. Approved. I'll order it.

Thursday, October 6. Quinn had booked the big room for the day and covered one wall in brown paper. Rafa's squad of nine stood in front of it with sticky notes, wearing the expressions of engineers who'd been told this would be fun.
The change board had approved the uncrewed option on Wednesday, as an option, in writing. Now somebody had to turn one sentence into work that a squad could finish two weeks at a time.

Haddad was on the screen from Houston with sticky notes of her own, which she held up to the camera one at a time. Overnight the station engineers had sent a packet listing what a lander would have to tell them after it touched down, and the list was longer than anyone at Watkins had expected.

Garrett's idea arrived at 8 AM, forwarded with no comment. Have Furrow do it. It'll write the stories overnight. Furrow was the code assistant Tallgrass had licensed for every engineer in July. It wrote code, it wrote tests, and according to the vendor's brochure it wrote user stories.

By four the wall has a spine across the top, one card per phase: depart, coast, correct, capture, hand off, land. Under each phase the cards get better as they go down, crude at the top and good at the bottom. The first row, the thinnest version of everything, is one sprint of work if they're lucky and two if they're honest. Every card has its acceptance criteria on the back in Haddad's words or the station's. Lander reports touchdown, attitude, and Breather bay temperature within ten minutes of landing. Rafa looks at the top row for a long time. That's a ship that's bad at everything. It's a ship that does everything, Haddad says. Badly. Then you make it good, and I watch.

Friday, October 7. Backlog refinement, the squad's word for the afternoon when they sat down with the product owner and argued about what was worth what. Haddad flew in that morning and came straight from the airport with her bag still on her shoulder.
At the top of the list were five items everybody agreed mattered and nobody agreed how much.

RELEASE A2 REFINEMENT TOP FIVE, NOT YET ORDERED. TIMING RACE IN THE GUIDANCE LOOP. KNOWN DEFECT FROM A1. FAILED RUN 2 ON SEPTEMBER 29.. SAFE MODE ON LOSS OF SIGNAL: HOLD ATTITUDE, KEEP THE BREATHER STACKS WARM, WAIT FOR THE GROUND.. TERMINAL DESCENT: HOVER AND TRANSLATE TO THE SITE.. BURN SUMMARY ON THE CREW DISPLAY AFTER CUTOFF. REQUESTED BY Y. HADDAD.. INVESTOR REPLAY MODE FOR RUN ONE, WITH NARRATION. REQUESTED BY THE OFFICE OF THE CEO.

Rafa wanted the descent first, because it was the hardest, and hard things were the fun ones. The two engineers who'd found the timing race wanted it fixed first, and said so in the tone people use when they've said a thing three times. Garrett's office had called twice about the replay mode, which had a date attached to it, because the investors met on November 15.
Haddad put her own card, the burn summary, face down on the table. Don't let me win because I'm holding the pen, she said. Tell me what each one costs us for every sprint we don't have it.

They score on the whiteboard, three columns for cost of delay and one for size. The timing race, small and in the way of everything, comes out on top by a mile. Safe mode second. The descent fourth on the raw score, behind Haddad's own summary. Haddad looks at that for a while and then does the thing Sam later writes to Ruth about. She marks the descent a must have for the release and her summary a should have, and moves her own card down below it. The formula's right about the order, she says. It doesn't know what the release is for. I do. The replay mode goes in as a won't have this time, with a note to Garrett's office explaining why, which Sam signs.

Monday, October 10. Sprint planning for A2-1, the release's first sprint, in the sim bay at 8 AM. By nine the squad had a sprint goal on the board, the guidance loop runs without the race, and the ship can keep itself safe when the ground goes quiet, and a forecast of thirty points, against a capacity Quinn had worked out to the person day.
Then they got to the definition of done, and Thandi Mokoena stood up.

Mokoena led the ARA's independent verification and validation team for Halcyon's software: five people in a trailer behind the sim bay, paid by the ARA, reporting to the agency's mission assurance office and to nobody at Tallgrass, which was the whole point of them. She'd been at the back of the room for all nine A1 runs, writing.
AUTONOMY SQUAD DEFINITION OF DONE REV 4 MAY 2061. CODE REVIEWED BY ONE OTHER SQUAD MEMBER.. UNIT TESTS WRITTEN AND PASSING.. MERGED TO THE RELEASE BRANCH.. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA MET.

Everything on that list happens inside the squad, Mokoena said. Nothing on it happens on the ship. A1 was done by this definition on September 23, and it flew once in nine. I'd like done to mean flown.
The integrated sim is a six hour run, Rafa said. Full regression is twenty two hours on the rig. Put that in done and half our points stop being done.

They rewrite it on the board. Rev 5 adds three lines: flown in the integrated sim against the stage and Breather models, with the run logged; reviewed against the requirement by someone outside the squad, from Mokoena's team; full regression passed on the rig. The forecast stays at thirty, because Mokoena's people run the reviews and the rig runs at night, but nothing counts until its logs are in, and Rafa says that's going to make Fridays very tense, and then says, more slowly, that it's the first definition he'd want on a ship his own kids were watching. Mokoena books the rig for every Wednesday night through March. Haddad, from the back, asks for one thing: that rev 5 be printed and posted in the sim bay where the crew trains, so they know what done means on their ship.

Saturday, October 15. Haddad's youngest played under eight soccer on Saturday mornings at a park in Aurora eleven blocks from Sam's house, which he hadn't known until she texted him a field number and asked if he'd come by. Field 6. Orange slices in a cooler. A man in a folding chair with a bullhorn he didn't need.

She stood on the sideline in a Halcyon fleece with her hands in her pockets and watched a seven year old in shin guards bigger than his legs miss the ball three times in a row with enormous confidence. That's Idris. He's going to be a goalkeeper. He doesn't know yet.

They watched for a while. Then, without looking at him: I ordered the uncrewed work last week. I put it where it goes. I'm good at my job. A whistle went. So I'd like you to tell me something, and I'd like it to be true. Are you planning to fly my ship without me?
Sam thought about the answer he'd have liked to give. Then he thought about a flight line in Arizona, a long time ago, and a signature he'd have given a lot for one more hour on.

We're planning for the day we'd have to, ma'am, Sam says. You break an ankle in January. A launch slips past March 4. The station can't wait twenty six months while we find you a replacement. You're the plan. This is what happens if the plan can't go. She doesn't say anything for long enough that Idris misses the ball again. Okay, she says. Then I'd like to write the rule for when it gets used. Before anybody needs it. With my crew. He says yes. On Monday there's a new card in her handwriting at the top of the backlog's governance column. CRITERIA FOR AN UNCREWED DEPARTURE. OWNER: HADDAD, WITH THE CREW AND THE BOARD. And under it, smaller: Written before we know the answer.

Monday, October 17. 5:40 AM. The two note chime. One way light time fourteen minutes and three seconds. He'd recorded his own log to her on Saturday night, after Field 6, and hadn't checked his hands.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3790. One way, 14 minutes 3 seconds. Margin, 680 days. Hi, Dad. Sol 3790. I have a guest. Say hi, Malik. He says hi. He's waving. He's nineteen and he waves like he's bringing in a plane. Malik's on my night shift now, Bay A and Bay C and, when nobody's looking, the other place. He's very good with the pumps and very bad with the plants. He talks to them. He says they like it. They do not like it, Malik. The basil is dying of your opinions. We made you a cooking show. This is Malik's recipe. One jalapeño. That's the recipe. There's a first green one on the plants I put in for Mom, and he wants to eat it, and I said he can have half if he says something nice about it on camera, so you'll know. Go. He says it's the best thing he's eaten in two years. Now he's crying, which is the jalapeño. Now he's coughing, which isn't. Okay. Go do the pumps. He's gone. I'll tell you now, because he made me promise not to tell his mom, and you're not his mom. He's had that cough for three weeks. Medical says it's the dust and the dry air in the night bays, and they're probably right. The good inhalers ran out in July. So he has the other kind, and it's fine, and he says it's fine, and at three in the morning I listen to him from the next bay. Don't tell Frances. I mean it, Dad. It's his to tell. But she's going to call you about something, she always does, and when she does you'll know this, and I'm sorry. Something else. Okonkwo's people listen to the loop recordings, the copies of Earth's voice loops that come up a day late in the morning packet, and on one of them they heard that Earth's building a ship that can fly itself. Half the station heard no doctor. The crew's bringing Dr. Rao, and everybody up here knows her name. If the ship can come without her, people want to know who decides that. I watched yours twice. You've got orange on your thumb. I want to know whose soccer game that was. 680. Same minus nine. Love you. Ada out.

He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on Malik's face in the middle of a laugh, because Frances had held a photograph of that face against her coat at the back of a briefing room in February, and in the photograph he'd been sixteen and had never coughed.
At 9:10 Frances Odum called his cell. Malik's mother didn't say hello. She never had.
It had started on the station, from a loop recording, and come down to Earth in the families' messages.

There's a story going around the families that the ship can come without its crew. Malik says the station's heard it too. I've got two hundred families asking me one thing, Mr. Okafor. If it comes without them, who brings the doctor?
A pause, and then the thing he'd been afraid she would say. And is there anything up there I should know about? Anything about my son?

The crew is the plan, ma'am, and Dr. Rao is on the crew, Sam says. We've looked hard at a way to get the plant there if the crew can't go, because the colony can't wait for the next window. If it's ever used, the board decides, on criteria written down before anybody needs them, and you'll hear it from me the same day. A breath. About your son. I can't speak for the station. I'd ask him. I'd ask him how he is, on a day when you've got time to hear the whole answer. The line is quiet for a long time. You know something, Frances says. I know he's the one to ask. That night he records a log to Ada and tells her Frances called, and what he said, and that he thinks Malik should be the one to tell her, and soon.

Wednesday, October 26. The October quarterly estimate was due to the partners on Monday the 31st, and Hale's chief of staff had called on Tuesday to ask for one line in it. The chief of staff's email came an hour later, so there'd be a record. The Director would like a date for the autonomy release that she can give the partners with confidence.
The option was in the release plan, declared, with Hana's word on it. The partners had read the word option, and now they wanted to know when.

The quarterly would carry the program's estimate at completion of 2,600 again, the number the Rule 4.2 notice had carried in July, against a budget of 2,472. The partners had funded the year's next tranche in August and would take up anything above the baseline against this estimate.

Quinn had the squad's numbers on one page. Five of the six sprints were measured under the old definition of done, she said. Rev 5 costs points. Whatever range I give you, read it wider than it looks.

Autonomy squad velocity, last six sprints (story points). Release A2 has 256 points left at the start of A2-2, Monday, October 24, refined and sized by the squad. Two week sprints, each ending on a Friday; A2-2 ends November 4.
Garrett had looked at it over Quinn's shoulder on his way past. Thirty seven. They did thirty seven once. Use that and put it in January. Partners love January.

Quinn writes the line herself and Sam signs it. Release A2: most likely Friday, February 24, 2062. Range February 10 to March 10, from the squad's last six sprints. Assumes the backlog doesn't grow. Growth or light holiday sprints push it toward March 10. Updated every second Friday, after the sprint review. Hale's chief of staff calls back to say the Director would prefer one date. Sam says he understands, that this is the line he can stand behind, and that the next update is November 4. Then Hale comes on the line herself. Then I'll say a range, she says. I've said worse things to eleven governments.
Tuesday, November 1. 9:40 PM. Sam was in his truck in the lot with the engine running when Mokoena called.

Under rev 5 the rig flew stories in the integrated sim on Wednesday nights, and on a Tuesday when the squad asked, for a story that wanted to be done by Friday. Tonight it was the first version of the terminal descent hover, merged on October 26. The squad's own tests were green. The story was one integrated run from done.

In the sim, the lander came down through the thin Martian air to four hundred meters, where the profile called for a hover, and didn't hover. It climbed. It climbed away from the landing site on seventy nine percent throttle, where Mars needed thirty, and ran out of propellant eleven hundred meters up, and fell.
By eleven Mokoena's team had found the line. In a routine called descent hover trim, one constant, G local, set to 9.80665. Standard gravity. Earth's, to six figures. Mars was about 3.73.

The routine had been written by Furrow. The engineer who'd asked for it, a guidance engineer eleven months on the program, had given it the hover code from the lander's tether tests at Watkins as an example, and it had done exactly what it was shown. It had also written the unit tests, from the same example, with the same number in them, and every one of them passed. One squad member had reviewed the merge. Mokoena's review was booked for Thursday, after the integrated run, which was the order rev 5 put them in.

The engineer was in the sim bay when Sam got there, sitting on the floor against the rig with his badge in both hands. Garrett had already texted from somewhere with music behind it. Was this the AI thing? Fix it tonight, don't make it a story.

By morning Mokoena's team and the squad have read every line Furrow wrote since July and found four more uses of 9.80665. Two are right, in the engine model, where standard gravity is how you turn specific impulse into thrust and is supposed to be Earth's. One is wrong, in a parachute deployment check nobody had flown yet. One is a comment. The routine comes out of the release branch at 2 AM. The corrected version, with the constant taken from the program's single constants file and tests written from the requirement by someone who didn't write the code, goes back in on Thursday. Sam writes the defect report himself at seven on Wednesday morning and sends it to the board's clerk and Hale's office before nine: what failed, how it was found, what's contained, what isn't known yet. The last line says the code was written by an AI assistant and accepted by people, and that the program's process let both of those happen. Then he finds the engineer, who's still in the building, and tells him what he wrote.

Thursday, November 3. 7:30 AM. Day nine of A2-2. The sprint review was Friday at two, with Haddad in the left seat and the readiness board's clerk in the back row, because the board had asked to see an autonomy increment at its November session and wanted a look first.
By Wednesday morning Mokoena's team and the squad had read every line Furrow had written since July. The parachute check was fixed too, and the defect report was with the board's clerk.
Quinn had the burndown up on the big screen in the sim bay, through the end of Wednesday.

Sprint A2-2 burndown: points remaining at the end of each day. Committed: 32 points over ten working days, Monday, October 24 to Friday, November 4. On day 8, Wednesday, five points of new work were added for the descent defect, and five points were finished. Left: the descent hover story, 5; safe mode, second slice (Breather thermal hold), 8; the downlink summary, 3; a constants cleanup, 1. Full regression on the rig takes twenty two hours.
Seventeen left and two days, Rafa said. And twenty two hours of regression that has to start by two this afternoon to be done by noon tomorrow. We're not going to make it.
Garrett, on the speaker: Run the new tests. The full suite passed two weeks ago. Nothing that old has changed.
The descent fix touched the constants file, Mokoena said. Everything reads the constants file.
Haddad was at Watkins on Thursdays now. She was standing by the door with a cardboard tray of coffee she'd brought for the squad, and she hadn't put it down.

Haddad puts the coffee down and they walk the burndown together. The descent hover is one integrated run from done, so its five points can finish before the regression has to start. She picks the descent hover, because it's the one the release can't do without and because the board's clerk will be watching for it. The second slice of safe mode, the Breather thermal hold, eight points, goes back to the top of the backlog for A2-3. So does the downlink summary, and the one point cleanup with it. The regression starts at 1:50. On Friday the squad shows twenty five points done, a smaller number than anybody wanted, and Haddad tells the room why before Rafa can. We found a defect on Tuesday, and we didn't hide it. That's what we did this sprint. It's what I'd want done on my ship.

Friday, November 4. At the review at two, before anything else, Rafa had flown the departure burn in the integrated sim twice, back to back, and it had flown twice. Afterward he wrote TWICE under ONCE on the sim bay door, smaller, and nobody said anything about it, which was how the squad celebrated.

3:30 PM, the retrospective, in the sim bay with the lights up. The squad, Haddad, Mokoena, Quinn, and two of Hana's engineers, because the constants file belonged to propulsion as much as anybody. Sam stood at the back by the door with his arms folded, because it wasn't his meeting.

Somebody had already written the defect's history on the whiteboard in a neat column, from the request to Furrow on Tuesday, October 25, to the run on Tuesday, November 1. Seven steps. At every one of them, somebody could have caught it.
Sam's defect report had gone to the board's clerk on Wednesday morning. The clerk had acknowledged it in capitals and put it on the agenda for the board's November session.
Garrett had sent one line at noon. Make sure we know who signed off on it.

They go down the column one step at a time, asking what made each step reasonable when it happened, and never who. The answers are ordinary and damning. The example Furrow was given came from Earth. The tests came from the same example. The review checklist had no line for constants. The outside review came after the integrated run, when it came at all. By five they have four changes, and Quinn writes them on one page. Every line of AI generated flight code is marked in its commit and reviewed by a named person who can explain it. Its tests are written from the requirement by somebody who didn't generate it. Constants come from the one program file and are never typed in. And Furrow stays, for what it's good at, which is a lot. The page goes into Tallgrass's software standard on Monday as revision 12, to every program in the company, and up to the station in the morning packet. The station's reply is one line. Q4. Understood as: you found it, and you told us how. We'd like to use this for the station's code. At 5:10 Sam answers Garrett's message from noon. All of us. It's fixed now.

Wednesday, November 16. The Independent Readiness Board's November session was in the room in the federal building downtown, with the same bad coffee and the same terrazzo in the hall. Item three on the agenda was a demonstration of the autonomy release, requested by the board, in a form left to the program. The sim bay couldn't come downtown, so there'd be a live link.

Garrett's office had a video ready: run one, from September, cut to four minutes with music under it. Hale's chief of staff had seen it and liked it. Rafa had a deck of velocity charts and burndowns, all of them honest. Mokoena had stopped by Sam's office on Monday with one question. What are you going to show them? The ship, or the team?
The full regression had run with the descent fix in it before the code went anywhere near a release. The squad had stopped talking about it, which Sam took as a good sign.
The containment had held. Every line Furrow had written since July had been read, by the squad and by Mokoena's team together, and the board had had Sam's report for two weeks.
Ruth was at the end of the bench with her green pen, three seats from the chair. She hadn't looked at him when he came in. She never did, in that room.

The link opens at ten. Rafa runs it from the sim bay, with Haddad in the left seat and her hands in her lap. Departure, clean. Coast, clean. Capture at Mars, crude, and it works. Then the descent, which hovers at thirty percent, and then fails the translate, on screen, in front of a federal board, because the translate is two sprints away. Rafa says so. Sam tells the defect story in four minutes: Earth's gravity in a Mars lander, a tool that did what it was shown, a review that didn't read the number, and what the squad did about it. Ruth Calder, who'd once been the Petrel's flight director, asks one question. How many times has it flown? The departure, twice in a row, Sam says. The rest, once each. That's what we've got. She writes it down. That afternoon the board's questions go into the backlog, eleven of them, ordered by Haddad, with the board named as the requester.

Monday, November 21. Page seven came in the mail on a gray afternoon with a Golden postmark, and the first snow of the season blowing sideways across the porch in Aurora. He read it at the kitchen table with his coat still on.
MAR 21 0930 ADMINISTRATOR ON THE LOOP: GOOD CALL, RUTHIE.

He read the 0715 line four times. APPROVED NEW TESTS ONLY. On November 3 he'd had his own version of that line, with smaller numbers in it, and Haddad had taken stories out of the sprint instead, and the squad had shown twenty five points to a room that wanted thirty two. It hadn't felt like a good call. It had felt like a Thursday.

The board's November minutes had a paragraph on the defect under the program's report, and a line at the end of it in the board's capitals: THE BOARD NOTES THAT THE PROGRAM'S REPORT WAS RECEIVED BEFORE ANY INQUIRY.
Tallgrass's software standard was at revision 12. Three other programs in the building had asked for the page, and one of them had found a constant of its own.

Haddad's card was still at the top of the governance column. CRITERIA FOR AN UNCREWED DEPARTURE. By Thanksgiving she'd written four of them with her crew, at her kitchen table in Aurora, and sent them to the board for its December session. The first one said: Only if no crew can go.

Ada's answer had come on October 19. Malik called his mom. He said she asked him how he was, and then she waited, and he told her. He's still coughing. She's still on Earth. But he's less alone with it, and so am I, and I didn't break a promise. Thanks for not making me.

On Quinn's integrated plan there was a milestone that hadn't been there in September, a diamond with a dashed line and the word OPTION beside it in capitals, Hana's word. Release A2, most likely February 24, range February 10 to March 10. It was the only thing on the plan that existed in case.

Thursday, November 24. Thanksgiving. He'd been asked to three houses and gone to none of them. At eight he sat at the kitchen table with a plate from the grocery store's hot counter and pressed record. One way light time fifteen minutes and thirty seconds. He told her about page seven, and Field 6, and the gravity constant, which she'd appreciate, because at twelve she'd lost a science fair to a units error and cried about it in the car all the way home.
He told her it had been a good two months, mostly, and then he told her the parts that hadn't been, because she'd ask.
He didn't do the voice. He sent it, and fifteen minutes and thirty seconds later it was on Mars.
Monday, November 28. 8:05 AM. Peg Sato from contracts came into his office without knocking, which she'd never done, put a folder on his desk, and sat down, which she'd also never done.
The folder was Aldergrove Fluid Systems blue, with the Pueblo address on the label. Inside was a letter on the company's letterhead, signed by Nell Garrity, requesting a change to the valve contract.

Aldergrove wants the root cause work pulled out of their fixed price. They put a number on it. I've read the number twice, once sitting down. She folded her glasses and set them on the folder. Garrett called me at six. He'd like to fire them.

Sam opened the folder. Under the letter somebody at Aldergrove had clipped a photocopy of a page from 2034, cold cycle data in faded columns, and beside the third row, in Nell's handwriting, two words: Still asking. He closed it again and put his hand flat on the cover, the way Quinn did, and thought about who in the building he had to talk to first. It wasn't Garrett.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 447. In the morning it would say 446, folder or no folder.
